Learning Objectives
Apply the philosophies and design principles of femoral fixation.
Review the surgical technique to improve the outcomes of various femoral component
designs.
Compare the indications for and outcomes of noncemented versus cemented femoral fixation
in primary hip arthroplasty.

The goal of total hip arthroplasty (THA) is to restore normal hip biomechanics with adequate
sizing, positioning, and fixation of prosthetic components while minimizing complications.1
Preoperative planning is essential (Video 1).
Understanding the principles of femoral fixation are essential for appropriate technique.
Video 1 Griffin WL: Primary total hip: Pre-operative planning and peri-operative management,
from Mason JB, mod: Primary total hip arthroplasty: Everything you need to know. Presented at
the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, San Diego, CA, March
14-18, 2017.
Femoral Fixation
Noncemented and cemented femoral designs are associated with excellent long-term results,
including in younger patients1, 2 (Resource 1)
Noncemented fixation predominates in North America and has increased globally.
Increased risk or periprosthetic fracture, early revision, and persistent thigh pain with
noncemented designs2, 3
Careful preoperative templating and radiographic evaluation of femoral anatomy are essential.


Femoral Fixation
Despite the increase in noncemented femoral fixation, outcome and registry data alone
do not support the shift to noncemented fixation. This may be related to surgeon
comfort and training and the push for efficiency in the operating room. Attention on
cemented fixation is renewed given the increasing age of the population and the rise in
early and late intraoperative and postoperative periprosthetic femur fracture associated
with the use of noncemented implants.4-9 Currently, periprosthetic fracture is a leading
cause of early revision after primary THA.9
Although the morbidity associated with cemented stems in elderly patients is a concern,
it is not well defined. The 2018 Australian Registry report described no difference in
overall mortality between cemented and noncemented fixation in patients aged 80 years
or older if corrected for Anesthesia Severity Score.3
Cemented Femoral Components
Polymethyl methacrylate has been used since it was pioneered by Charnley in the 1960s.
Cemented implants continue to be commonly used, resulting in excellent long-term outcomes
and survivorship.3
General Principles10
Two philosophies for cemented femoral fixation exist.3, 10-12
A taper-slip prosthesis allows for controlled subsidence in the cement.
A composite-beam structure allows the stem to function as a unit within the cement.
Improved implant-to-cement adhesion is provided by increased surface roughness.12
Rounded edges are favored over sharp edges.

General Principles
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:51 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis: Femoral Component
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004100
3/26

The taper-slip concept involves the use of a dual- or triple-taper stem with a smooth or
highly polished surface finish, allowing the stem to wedge into the cement mantle over
the course of the first postoperative year, which improves proximal loading of the
cement mantle. The composite-beam concept relies on a strong bond between the stem
and the cement; therefore, the two different materials function as a single unit during
load transmission. Stems that rely on the composite-beam principle usually are
roughened or matted to maximize the mechanical strength of the bond between the
cement mantle and the stem. A collar may improve survivorship of composite-beam
fixation by improving proximal loading and resisting subsidence. Cemented stem cross-
sectional shape influences the cement mantle thickness surrounding it and stress
transfer.13 Rectangular and oval cross-sectional shape are commonly used in clinical
practice. Although rectangular stems offer more rotational stability, the edges can create
stress risers.11 Rounded edges are favored over sharp corners that occur at transition
points and are less likely to produce stress risers. Areas of increased stress
concentration may lead to microfractures of the cement mantle, which may adversely
affect the durability of the cement mantle11 (Figure 1; Resource 2).
Figure 1

Outcomes
Polished stems tend to result in better outcomes than roughened/matte surface finishes.
Debonded, rough components produce abundant wear debris and severe osteolysis.
Smooth and highly polished cemented stems produce little debris.
Fatigue fractures (cracks between preexisting pores in the cement mantle) are the primary
mode of component failure.
Polished tapered stems are associated with improved survivorship compared with collared
composite-beam implants.

Outcomes
The risk of micromotion between the stem and the cement mantle increases with
repetitive axial and rotational forces over time; this phenomenon is well tolerated in
polished tapered stems but can result in failure in stems with a matte finish.14 If the
bond between the stem and cement breaks in a patient with a roughened/matte
composite-beam stem, micromotion can occur, resulting in abrasive wear of the cement
mantle and leading to osteolysis and aseptic loosening.15 Therefore, polished stems
generally are associated with better clinical survivorship than stems of the same
geometry with a roughened/matt surface finish.14 Stem subsidence of 1 to 2 mm over
the first postoperative year commonly is noted around the shoulder of collarless,
polished tapered stems and does not suggest loosening or impending failure of femoral
reconstruction.11
In considering the two main cemented femoral stem designs, some variation exists in
outcomes. The outcomes of collared, composite-beam implants are listed in Table 1.16,
27-32
.

Polished tapered stems demonstrate markedly improved survivorship compared with
collared, composite-beam implants. An Australian Registry study showed a substantially
lower cumulative rate of revision with polished stems compared with collared,
composite-beam implants.17 This difference was evident in patients younger than 75
years and became apparent at midterm follow-up and continued to increase with time.17
Although both stem designs were associated with excellent early to midterm results, the
long-term survivorship of polished stems was considerably better than that of
composite-beam implants because of the lower incidence of aseptic loosening, which
also has been confirmed by data from other registries.17, 18 This has been extrapolated
to younger patients with pathology other than osteoarthritis, such as osteonecrosis and
inflammatory arthritis.19 Knowledge of the underlying principles behind stem design and
function will help surgeons appropriately select and use cemented implants to maximize
outcomes.

Indications
Applicable for most patients undergoing hemiarthroplasty or THA
Consider in patients 70 years or older
Patients with risk factors for postoperative periprosthetic femur fracture, inflammatory
arthritis, femoral neck fracture, conversion of failed hip fixation
History of metabolic bone disease or fragility fracture, especially osteoporosis
Dorr type C bone20

Indications
Cemented femoral fixation remains the superior option in patients with poor bone stock
who are at risk for postoperative periprosthetic femur fracture after primary THA.
Cemented femoral components are associated with decreased perioperative
complications, improved functional recovery, and decreased pain in elderly patients and
patients with poor bone quality who undergo THA.21
The Dorr classification system involves the use of plain radiographs to assess the bone
quality of the proximal femur. Surgeons must evaluate lateral radiographs.8, 9 Dorr type
C bone, described as stovepipe, is associated with complete loss of the medial and
posterior cortices.
Contraindications
Bleeding dyscrasias
Bone marrow disorder

Severe pulmonary disease (relative contraindication)
Technique (Video 2)
Templating of the contralateral hip aids in selection of an appropriately sized femoral
component with the desired offset.
Cemented stems are associated with more control over stem version than noncemented
implants that rely on proximal metaphyseal fixation.
Modern cementation techniques: porosity reduction, pressurization, pulsatile lavage, and
distal centralization
Vacuum mixing diminishes cement porosity and increases fatigue strength.
The highest intramedullary pressures are achieved during cemented stem insertion.
Exposure of supportive cancellous bone and bone irrigation and drying before cementation as
well as sustained pressurization until cement cures after cementation are key elements in
producing an excellent cement mantle.
Video 2 Lachiewicz PF: Indications and Techniques for Total Hip Arthroplasty Cemented Femoral
Component [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2008.


Technique
Modern cementation technique involves the use of cement restrictors, pulsatile lavage, a
cement gun with a long nozzle, a foam pressurizer, and distal centralizers to improve the
quality of the cement mantle and positioning of the implant. Bone preparation and the
timing of cement/stem insertion are important aspects of the technique that are critical
for excellent prosthetic fixation.
During preoperative templating, most templates allow surgeons to plan for a 2- to 4-mm
cement mantle with an outer 3 to 4 mm of cancellous bone supportive of the femoral
metaphysis.
Cemented stems allow for more control over stem version than noncemented implants
because of the variability in native femoral anteversion. The additional freedom to adjust
component version within the cement mantle allows surgeons to control another
parameter to minimize the risk of dislocation.
A summary of the steps for femoral preparation and cemented stem insertion is listed in
Table 2.

Complications
Bone-cement implantation syndrome (BCIS) presents as hypoxia, hypotension, and/or sudden
cardiovascular collapse during or briefly after pressurization of cement into the femoral canal.
BCIS is believed to be the combined result of fat and marrow embolization, pulmonary
hypertension, right heart strain/failure, and methyl methacrylate monomer release into
circulation.
Recommendations have been made to mitigate the effects of BCIS, including adequate volume
maintenance, thorough irrigation of the femoral canal before instrumentation, avoidance of
over-pressurization of the cement in susceptible patients, cement placement later in the

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004100
10/26

curing phase, and slow insertion of the femoral stem. If a long-cemented stem is used, venting
of the femoral canal should be considered.

Complications
BCIS was initially described by Donaldson et al22 in 2009, with the establishment of a
grading system for BCIS severity. BCIS is incompletely understood; however, it is
postulated to result from several factors, with possible immunologic response from
compliment activation, histamine release, and endogenous cannabinoid-mediated
vasodilation.
In response to the risks associated with bone cement, recommendations were made by
United Kingdom orthopaedic, anesthetic, and geriatric groups to mitigate the effect of
bone cement on patients undergoing cemented femoral technique (Table 3). Although
maintenance of adequate intravascular volume before and during cementation may
appear to minimize the effects of bone cement, it may not entirely prevent BCIS.
Additional research is required on the higher rates of BCIS in patients with a femoral
neck fracture. Maximal medical optimization and astute intraoperative anesthetic co-
management are crucial to avoid hypoxia and hypotension in this subset of higher risk
patients.
Although the practice of using noncemented stems in THA currently is common in the
United States, cemented stems are associated with good long-term outcomes in all age
groups and a decreased risk of early postoperative periprosthetic femur fracture.

Notify the anesthetic team of the timing of cementation.
Perform thorough irrigation of the femoral canal before instrumentation
Avoid over-pressurization of the cement in susceptible patients.
Use suction catheters and cement restrictors.

Noncemented Femoral Components
Concerns for cement failure led to the increase in noncemented or porous metal press-fit
fixation.
Noncemented fixation is a biologic fixation.
Various surfaces and materials can be used in noncemented fixation.
The shape of the implant determines the location of bony contact and subsequent fixation.
Long-term results are excellent3, 23, 33-38 (Table 4).

General Principles
Design features/implant shapes include tapered, cylindrical, and anatomic stems16 (Figure 2).
Initial stability is essential for subsequent osteointegration.
Micromotion of less than 28 μm is essential for bone formation.24
Thigh pain was common with earlier designs; modifications in shape and material were made
to address this complication.
Distally engaged stems may lead to proximal stress shielding.

Figure 2
Photographs show implant designs used in noncemented fixation. A, A tapered stem designed to
engage the metaphyseal cortical bone medial to lateral and anterior to posterior for implant
stability. Typically, the coating is on the proximal one-third of the implant. (Bi-Metric femoral
implant, Zimmer Biomet). B, A cylindrical prosthesis designed to engage the diaphyseal cortical


General Principles
Initial implant stability is obtained via a press-fit or scratch-fit. Micromotion of more than
150 μm results in fibrous tissue formation. If micromotion of 30 to 150 μm is present, a
combination of bone and fibrous tissue formation will occur.

15/26

Stiffness of the stem has been associated with increased stress shielding and modulus
mismatch. Stem modifications include the use of titanium and attempts to decrease the
stem radius.
Surfaces and Coatings
Circumferential coating is essential for long-term outcomes.
Osseointegration depends on a porous or roughened metal surface.
Ongrowth occurs on roughened or textured surfaces.
Ingrowth occurs with pore sizes between 50 and 400 μm and a porosity of 40% to 50%.24

Surfaces and Coatings
Ingrowth surfaces include sintered beads, fiber mesh, and porous metals. Ongrowth
surfaces include those that are grit-blasted or plasma-sprayed.
Circumferential coating is essential for long-term outcomes. This affords enhanced
fixation, results in less stress shielding, and serves as a seal against distal osteolysis.25
Tapered Stems
Tapered stems have a proximal-to-distal taper that is designed to interlock in the metaphysis
with no diaphyseal fixation.
The implant usually is collarless, allowing the prosthesis to be wedged into the bony
metaphysis, providing optimal fit and bone ingrowth.
The tapered design allows for subsidence into a tight fit and optimizes proximal load sharing
of the implant, thereby optimizing bone ingrowth and minimizing stress shielding.
Single-tapered stems (also known as single-wedge stems) are tapered and engage only in the
mediolateral plane.
Dual-tapered stems (or dual-wedge stems) taper and engage in the mediolateral and
anteroposterior planes.
Tapered stems were designed for more proximal bone loading to decrease stress shielding.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:51 PM

Indications
Tapered stems are indicated for Dorr type A and type B bone and in younger patients.20
Contraindications
Osteopenic bone, Dorr type C bone20
In Dorr type A bone, a mismatch in which the thickened cortices and the narrow canal do not
accommodate the distal portion of the stem may occur. In these canals, a metaphyseal and
diaphyseal mismatch exists.
Technique
Osteotomize the femoral neck at the level of preoperative templating.
A box osteotome can be used to remove the lateral neck and bone medial to trochanter to
avoid varus positioning.
A straight canal seeker can be used to identify the canal.
Sequential reaming usually is not necessary.
For optimal sizing, broaching should occur in the central portion of the canal.
Sequential broaching is performed to engage the medial and lateral endosteal cortices.
During broaching, appropriate version should be maintained on impaction and extraction of
the broach.
If the broach is stable and does not advance axial impaction, a change in pitch often is noted.
The broach also should be rotationally stable.
Trial reduction can be performed to assess leg length and stability.
The actual prosthesis, which is slightly oversized, is then impacted in place.
Primary THA with the use of double-tapered stems is discussed in Resource 3.26
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Cortical perforation can be avoided by using a canal finder, attaining appropriate exposure
centering in the canal, and being cognizant of alignment.
Under-sizing of the component and correlation with templated size: ensure central positioning
in the canal in the anteroposterior plane, lateralize to ensure not in varus, consider
interoperative imaging
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:51 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004100
17/26

Outcomes
Excellent long-term clinical outcomes and survivorship
99.4% survivorship for short, tapered stems at a follow-up of 7 years (Resource 4)
98% survivorship for second-generation single-tapered stems at a follow-up of 20 years; this is
attributed to the inherent stability of the design, which facilitates immediate initial fixation and
potent osseointegration along the proximal coating
95.7% to 100% survivorship for dual-tapered stems at a follow-up of 15 years, with less stress-
shielding and thigh pain than that with cylindrical, fully coated stems24
Cylindrical Stems
Straight stems that engage the cortices of the diaphysis (Resource 5)
Initial stability depends on a tight diaphyseal fit.
The tubular diaphysis can be reproducibly machined to allow for a tight fit and subsequent
bone ingrowth. This is accomplished via the slightly oversized textured implant obtaining a
scratch-fit in the endosteal cortex of the diaphysis.
These stems are associated with higher rates of thigh pain and stress shielding than tapered
stems because of distal fixation and loading.
A proximal and distal coating optimizes the surface area for maximum bone ingrowth.
These stems typically have a collar to load the medial cortex.
Indications
Cylindrical stems are indicated in Dorr type A and type B bone and in younger patients.20
Contraindications
Exercise caution in osteopenic bone, Dorr type C bone.20
Avoid large diameter implants in thin, widened cortices.
Technique
Osteotomize the femoral neck at the level of preoperative templating.
A box osteotome can be used to remove the lateral neck and bone medial to trochanter to
avoid varus positioning.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:51 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis: Femoral Component
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004100
18/26

A straight canal finder can be used to identify the canal.
Sequential reaming is performed and proceeds in 0.5-mm increments.
Removal of bone from the medial aspect of the base of the greater trochanter is important to
ensure a direct path into the canal. A lateralizing proximal reamer may be used.
The appropriate size is reached if cortical engagement is noted. This is detected by a resistance
to the reamer, an auditory change, and cortical bone noted in the reamer flutes.
The femur is then broached to the corresponding size, with attention to version of the
component.
Trial reduction can be performed.
The actual prosthesis, which is slightly oversized, is then impacted into place.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Eccentric reaming and varus positioning: Ensure removal of lateral proximal bone
Risk of intraoperative periprosthetic fracture: Impact the actual prosthesis with a consistent
force
Outcomes
Excellent long-term, revision-free outcomes
100% and 97.8% survivorship at a follow-up of 11.4 years and 20 years, respectively.
Mean bone mineral density is lower with extensively coated stems than in contralateral
controls; however, no correlation exists with Harris hip scores and pain.24
Modular Stems
Modular designs allow for independent metaphyseal and diaphyseal preparation and offer
combined proximal and distal fixation (Resource 6).
This flexibility is an option for rotational or anatomic variations observed in patients with hip
dysplasia.23
These designs typically consist of a metaphyseal sleeve and a modular diaphyseal stem.
The diaphysis is initially reamed, and a stem is placed.
Proximal preparation is completed by reaming over the stem to achieve cortical contact for the
metaphyseal sleeve.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:51 PM

Indications
Noncemented fixation is warranted.
Commonly used in patients with dysplasia, patients with proximal femur deformity, and
revision settings.
Contraindications
Exercise caution in osteopenic bone, Dorr type C bone.20
Technique
Osteotomize the femoral neck at the level of preoperative templating.
A box osteotome can be used to remove the lateral neck and bone medial to trochanter to
avoid varus positioning.
A straight canal finder can be used to identify the canal.
Sequential distal reaming is performed until cortical engagement occurs. This is detected by a
resistance to the reamer, an auditory change, and cortical bone noted in the reamer flutes.
The reamer is left in place distally, and a proximal reamer is used to machine the metaphyseal
portion of the stem.
Trial components are assembled, and reduction is performed.
The actual prosthesis, which is slightly oversized, is then impacted into place.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Eccentric reaming and varus positioning: Ensure removal of lateral proximal bone
Risk of intraoperative periprosthetic fracture: Impact the actual prosthesis with consistent
force (Table 4)23
84% to 94% survivorship at a follow-up of 10 to 11 years for stems with a modular body;
however, long-term results are sparse.
Mark as Complete
